stem: In **hypertrophied hearts**, what did myocardial pH measurements show when **continuous antegrade cold blood cardioplegia** was compared with **intermittent cold cardioplegia**?

choices.text: The myocardial milieu was equally abnormal with both methods
The myocardial milieu became completely normal with continuous perfusion
The myocardial milieu was more normal, but not completely normal, with continuous perfusion
The myocardial milieu was more normal with intermittent cold cardioplegia
The myocardial milieu was more normal with continuous perfusion only when given retrograde

explanation.text: Myocardial pH data showed that, at least in **hypertrophied hearts**, the myocardial milieu is ==more normal, although not completely normal==, with continuous antegrade cold blood cardioplegia than with intermittent cold cardioplegia.

explanation.caption: Continuous cold cardioplegic perfusion
head: Route
What the chapter reports
rows: Alternative to single-dose and multidose intermittent cold cardioplegia; myocardial milieu more normal (not completely normal) in hypertrophied hearts
**Retrograde** continuous cold via the coronary sinus
Clinical experience: an excellent method of myocardial management; some give it after an initial antegrade cold dose
Retrograde cold blood after initial antegrade cold blood
_Experimentally_ found to maintain optimal myocardial pH

explanation.title: Better, not perfect
explanation.text: Continuous perfusion improved the milieu but did **not** make it completely normal.
the myocardial milieu is more normal, although not completely normal, with this method than with intermittent cold cardioplegia.

choiceNotes.a: The milieu was **more normal** with continuous perfusion, not equally abnormal.
choiceNotes.b: The source stresses it was **not completely normal**.

stem: A surgeon considers **continuous warm blood cardioplegia** for a CABG. Which statement best summarizes how the chapter assesses this technique?

choices.text: It gives good protection but is surgically inconvenient for certain operations
It is given without an initial antegrade dose, by the retrograde route only
It has been consistently superior to intermittent cold cardioplegia in all reports
It is limited to CABG and has not been used for other cardiac operations
It has been abandoned because its myocardial protection is poor

explanation.text: Continuous warm blood cardioplegia ==provides good myocardial protection==, but it is ==surgically inconvenient for certain operations==.

items: **Delivery**: antegrade or retrograde coronary sinus infusion **after an initial antegrade dose**.
**Use**: CABG **and other** cardiac operations.
**Evidence is mixed**: some found ventricular function recovery better than with intermittent cold cardioplegia; others found similar efficacy between warm and cold.

choiceNotes.b: It is given antegrade **or** retrograde, and **after an initial antegrade dose**.
choiceNotes.c: Results are mixed: some groups found better recovery, others **similar efficacy** between warm and cold.

stem: Which property does the chapter attribute to **cold cardioplegia with controlled aortic root reperfusion** (and warm cardioplegic induction when needed)?

choices.text: It markedly prolongs the operation compared with standard cardioplegia
It is frequently complicated by ventricular fibrillation during reperfusion
Its advantages have been clearly proven, so it is now used almost universally
It is best reserved for complex high-risk operations only
It is essentially devoid of ventricular fibrillation and minimizes stunning

explanation.text: The technique is ==essentially devoid of ventricular fibrillation==, ==minimizes myocardial stunning and necrosis==, is surgically convenient and prolongs the operation only mildly.

steps.text: Belief: control of **all aspects of reperfusion** may matter more than details of cold cardioplegia
During reperfusion the heart is **separated from events in the rest of the body** for a brief time

steps.label: result
steps.text: Less VF, less stunning and necrosis, apparently better postoperative cardiac performance

explanation.title: Not proven, not universal
items: Proof of its advantages has been **as difficult to obtain** as for other techniques, so it is **not yet widely used in its entirety**.

explanation.title: Circuitry
explanation.text: A small **separate system** on the pump-oxygenator, with its own **miniaturized heat exchanger and two pumps**, delivers the solution at controlled temperature and pressure (aortic root, retrograde, or both).
The technique is surgically convenient, prolongs the operation only mildly, is essentially devoid of ventricular fibrillation, minimizes myocardial stunning and myocardial necrosis

stem: After completing a CABG in an adult, with the aortic clamp still in place, controlled **warm aortic root reperfusion** with hyperkalemic, modified, enriched blood cardioplegia is begun. Which **aortic root pressure** sequence is recommended?

choices.text: 50 to 75 mmHg for the first 60 to 120 seconds, then 30 mmHg
30 mmHg for the first 60 to 120 seconds, then 50 to 75 mmHg
30 mmHg maintained throughout the entire reperfusion
100 mmHg for the first 60 to 120 seconds, then 50 to 75 mmHg
50 to 75 mmHg for the first 60 to 120 seconds, then 100 mmHg

explanation.title: Warm terminal reperfusion ("hot shot"), clamp on

steps.text: **Warm, hyperkalemic, modified, enriched** blood cardioplegia into the aortic root

steps.label: then
steps.text: Root pressure **50–75 mmHg** in adults (infants/children with BSA < 1 m^2^: normal systemic arterial diastolic pressure)

steps.label: total
steps.text: **500 mL** of modified reperfusate (scaled down if BSA < 1.5 m^2^)

choiceNotes.e: The sequence starts at **30 mmHg** and rises to 50–75 mmHg, not to 100 mmHg.

stem: A child with a body surface area (BSA) of **0.75 m^2^** has an elective intracardiac repair under cardioplegia. What **volume of warm modified blood reperfusate** should be given for the terminal warm reperfusion?

375 mL
125 mL
250 mL
750 mL

Rule
rows: Root pressure after first 60–120 s (infants/children, BSA < 1 m^2^)

stem: After the warm terminal reperfusate ("hot shot") has been infused, controlled aortic root perfusion is continued with the **aortic clamp still in place**. Which perfusate is used, and what must the surgeon concentrate on during this phase?

choices.text: Normothermic, normokalemic, unmodified blood; avoiding ventricular distention
Warm, hyperkalemic, enriched blood; avoiding ventricular distention
Cold, hyperkalemic blood cardioplegia; avoiding myocardial rewarming
Normothermic, normokalemic, unmodified blood; keeping root pressure near 120 mmHg
Cold crystalloid cardioplegia; avoiding ventricular fibrillation

explanation.text: The circuit is switched to ==normothermic, normokalemic, unmodified blood==, and the surgeon must concentrate on ==avoiding ventricular distention==.

items: The heart stays **flaccid and electromechanically quiescent for 2 to 10 minutes** after the onset of controlled root reperfusion.
**Coronary resistance may rise** during this time → the perfusionist **reduces the flow rate** to keep a **constant aortic root pressure**.
The adverse effects of ventricular distention have been fully documented.

explanation.title: Two different reperfusates
explanation.text: Warm **hyperkalemic** modified blood is the initial 500-mL terminal reperfusate; what follows with the clamp on is **normokalemic, unmodified** blood.

choiceNotes.b: Warm hyperkalemic enriched blood is the **initial** terminal reperfusate; afterwards the perfusate is **normokalemic, unmodified** blood.
choiceNotes.c: Cold cardioplegia is not given during controlled reperfusion; the blood is **normothermic**.
choiceNotes.d: Root pressure must be kept from becoming excessively high (> 120 mmHg); 120 mmHg is not a target.
choiceNotes.e: Blood, not crystalloid, is used; and the surgeon's focus is **ventricular distention**.

stem: During controlled aortic root reperfusion, the period of electromechanical quiescence passes and cardiac action begins. What is the **initial rhythm** most frequently seen?

choices.text: Ventricular fibrillation
Sinus rhythm with strong contractions
Atrioventricular (AV) dissociation
Persistent asystole needing pacing
Ventricular tachycardia

explanation.text: When cardiac action begins, the initial rhythm ==frequently is AV dissociation==; ==very rarely== it is ventricular fibrillation.

steps.text: **Sinus rhythm** with **strong contractions** = endpoint (usually 10–25 min from start)

choiceNotes.b: Sinus rhythm with strong contractions is the **endpoint** reached later, not the initial rhythm.

stem: During controlled aortic root perfusion, cardiac action has resumed. Even the vented left ventricle ejects blood into the isolated aortic root, and the **aortic root pressure rises toward 130 mmHg**. What is the appropriate response?

choices.text: Release the aortic clamp immediately
Stop small-volume pulmonary ventilation
Increase the aortic root perfusion flow rate
Give a further dose of warm hyperkalemic reperfusate
Reduce root perfusion flow, adding suction on the root pressure catheter if needed

explanation.text: The perfusionist must ==reduce the aortic root perfusion flow rate== to keep root pressure from becoming excessively high (**> 120 mmHg**), and at times places ==suction on the aortic root pressure catheter==.

steps.label: fix
steps.text: **Reduce root flow** ± suction on root pressure catheter

choiceNotes.a: Controlled root perfusion continues until sinus rhythm and strong contractions return; the clamp is released later, after de-airing maneuvers.

choiceNotes.c: Increasing flow would raise root pressure further; flow must be **reduced**.
choiceNotes.d: The hyperkalemic reperfusate is the initial step; now the perfusate is normokalemic blood and the problem is excessive pressure.

stem: Normal immature hearts tolerate ischemia relatively well. For a **cyanotic neonate in heart failure** coming to open heart surgery, what does the chapter conclude about the heart's tolerance of global myocardial ischemia?

By adding calcium to the CPB prime

explanation.text: Reoxygenation injury ==may be avoidable by beginning CPB at the ambient oxygen tension of the hypoxemic subject==.

steps.label: sudden reoxygenation on CPB
steps.text: ↑ Conjugated dienes, **hydroxyl radicals** → lipid peroxidation, nitric oxide release

explanation.title: Experimental adjuncts
explanation.text: Adding **deferoxamine** and antioxidants (such as catalase and coenzyme Q10) to the prime might limit oxidant damage; their importance in human neonates is **not yet clarified**.
This hypoxemic/reoxygenation injury may be avoidable by beginning CPB at the ambient oxygen tension of the hypoxemic subject.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.a: Abrupt reoxygenation is the **cause** of the injury; CPB should begin at the patient's ambient oxygen tension.
choiceNotes.c: The injury arises from reoxygenation during the **initial stages of CPB**, not from cross-clamp timing.
choiceNotes.d: Reoxygenation injury is addressed through the oxygen tension at CPB start; one study even found cold **blood** cardioplegia superior to crystalloid St. Thomas solution in infants.
choiceNotes.e: The suggested prime additives are **deferoxamine and antioxidants**; the immature heart is at risk of calcium overload.

topic: Neonates and Infants: del Nido Cardioplegia
stem: **del Nido cardioplegic solution** is based on the extracellular composition of the Buckberg solutions. Which modification, with its rationale, is correct?

choices.text: Higher calcium, because pediatric myocardium relies on calcium flux
Lower magnesium, to allow faster return of excitability
Mannitol added as the main arresting agent
Lidocaine added to block sodium channels and limit early reperfusion calcium overload
Glutamate and aspartate added as the main arresting agents

explanation.text: **Lidocaine** is added to ==block sodium channels==, reducing cell excitability and ==limiting calcium overload during early reperfusion==.

explanation.caption: del Nido vs Buckberg base: major differences
head: Change
Reason
rows: Pediatric myocardium relies more on calcium flux for EC coupling and tolerates postischemic calcium overload poorly
Further depresses cell excitability (and metabolism, ATP use) during ischemia
Sodium channel block → less excitability, less calcium overload in early reperfusion

explanation.title: Table 3.1 roles
items: **Potassium chloride**: depolarizes the cell membrane
**Lidocaine**: maintains arrest in a hyperpolarized state
**Magnesium**: calcium channel blocker, prevents contractile activation
**Mannitol**: decreases edema, free radical scavenger

explanation.text: Lidocaine is added to block sodium channels; this reduces cell excitability and limits calcium overload during early reperfusion.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.a: Calcium is **lower** in del Nido solution, precisely because pediatric myocardium tolerates postischemic calcium overload poorly.
choiceNotes.b: Magnesium is **increased** to depress cell excitability further.
choiceNotes.c: Mannitol decreases myocardial edema and scavenges free radicals; potassium, lidocaine and magnesium are the arresting agents.
choiceNotes.e: Glutamate and aspartate are discussed for warm induction and reperfusate in experimental studies, not as del Nido arresting agents.

topic: Neonates and Infants: del Nido Cardioplegia
stem: A neonate is to receive **del Nido cardioplegia**. Which description of its preparation and use is correct?

choices.text: One part solution to four parts blood; induction 20 mL/kg; redosing every 20 to 30 minutes
Four parts solution to one part blood; induction 30 mL/kg; redosing every 20 to 30 minutes
Pure crystalloid without blood; induction 20 mL/kg; redosing intervals up to 90 minutes
One part solution to four parts blood; induction 30 mL/kg; redosing intervals up to 90 minutes
Four parts solution to one part blood; induction 20 mL/kg; redosing intervals up to 90 minutes

explanation.text: del Nido solution is mixed ==4 parts solution : 1 part blood==; induction follows the ==20 mL/kg== Boston dose; recommended intervals between doses are ==up to 90 min== (vs 20–30 min for Buckberg).

head: Item
del Nido
rows: Additional induction up to **30 cc/kg** (center dependent)
Faster return of sinus rhythm; shorter cross-clamp times and fewer doses; most common formulation in a CHSS survey (**38%**)

explanation.text: The del Nido cardioplegic solution (Baxter) is combined with blood in a ratio of four parts solution to one part blood.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.a: The ratio is **4 solution : 1 blood**, and redosing intervals are up to 90 min (20–30 min applies to Buckberg).
choiceNotes.b: 30 mL/kg is the **additional** induction for hypertrophied hearts; intervals are up to 90 min.
choiceNotes.c: del Nido solution is **combined with blood** (4:1).
choiceNotes.d: The ratio is reversed and 30 mL/kg is used only for hypertrophied hearts.

stem: A patient with **severe aortic stenosis** and marked left ventricular hypertrophy undergoes aortic valve replacement. What is the **single most important change** in myocardial management?

choices.text: Increasing the amount of cardioplegia given
Using retrograde cardioplegia as the only route
Using crystalloid instead of blood cardioplegia
Lengthening the interval between reinfusions to 60 minutes
Lowering the cardioplegic flow to protect the subendocardium

explanation.text: Because of high heart weight and severe hypertrophy with difficult subendocardial perfusion, the single most important change is to ==increase the amount of cardioplegia given==.

items: Blood cardioplegia **> 300 mL/min for 5 min**.
**Antegrade and retrograde** delivery.
Reinfusion **after 20 minutes**, also at higher volumes (**250–300 mL/min**).

explanation.text: **Any incomplete delivery** of cardioplegia must be avoided and will result in myocardial damage.
Myocardial management must be adapted to this special situation with a significantly higher heart weight, severe hypertrophy, and, consequently, difficult perfusion of the subendocardial layer.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 103

choiceNotes.b: The example uses **antegrade and retrograde** delivery.
choiceNotes.c: The example given is **blood** cardioplegia at higher volumes.
choiceNotes.d: Reinfusion is given **after 20 minutes**.
choiceNotes.e: Flow is **increased** (> 300 mL/min) because subendocardial perfusion is difficult.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A patient needing aortic valve replacement has **mild aortic regurgitation**. Initial cardioplegia is infused antegrade through the unopened aortic root, and **root pressure stays adequate**, confirming minimal runoff. What is done next?

choices.text: An aortotomy is made at once and the infusion is switched to the coronary ostia
Left atrial vent suction is increased and the infusion is stopped
The left atrial vent is clamped, the infusion continues, and the LV is gently massaged
The infusion is switched to the retrograde route only
The aortic clamp is released briefly to decompress the ventricle

explanation.text: With adequate root pressure, the ==left atrial vent line is clamped==, the infusion continues, and the ==left ventricle is gently massaged== manually; this prevents LV distention and helps perfuse the coronary arteries.

explanation.title: Mild AR: initial antegrade infusion via unopened root

branches.label: adequate (minimal runoff)
branches.text: Clamp LA vent, continue infusion, **gently massage LV**

explanation.text: Unless the aortic valve is completely competent (uncommon), induction for aortic valve repair or replacement is best by **direct ostial infusion preceded by retrograde induction** via the coronary sinus.
the left atrial vent line is clamped, the infusion continues, and the left ventricle is gently massaged manually during the infusion period.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 103

choiceNotes.a: An aortotomy with direct ostial infusion is for **excessive runoff**; here runoff is minimal.
choiceNotes.b: The LA vent line is **clamped** and the infusion **continues**.
choiceNotes.d: With adequate root pressure the antegrade infusion simply **continues**.
choiceNotes.e: Distention is prevented by **manual LV massage**, not clamp release.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: During aortic valve surgery, after brief electrical fibrillation the aorta is clamped and antegrade cardioplegia is started, but **aortic root pressure is below 50 mmHg**. In the sequence described, what follows?

choices.text: Increase antegrade root flow until root pressure exceeds 100 mmHg
Start retrograde cardioplegia at > 300 mL/min and open the aorta for ostial cannulation
Stop all cardioplegia and cool the patient systemically to 20°C
Continue antegrade root infusion and massage the left ventricle
Release the aortic clamp and repeat induction after defibrillation

explanation.text: If root pressure is ==< 50 mmHg==, ==retrograde cardioplegia is started at > 300 mL/min== and the proximal aorta is opened with a **hockey-stick incision** for coronary ostial cannulae.

steps.text: Brief electrical VF → aortic clamp → antegrade cardioplegia

steps.label: ostial cannulae
steps.text: Left 2 min then right 2 min, **or** both simultaneously; retrograde stopped once antegrade established

steps.label: maintenance
steps.text: Reinfusions every **20–25 min** (retrograde, antegrade or simultaneous)

explanation.text: Once antegrade cardioplegic perfusion has been established, retrograde delivery is stopped.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 103

choiceNotes.a: Low root pressure here prompts **retrograde** delivery and direct ostial cannulation, not higher root flow.
choiceNotes.c: Systemic cooling to 20°C is the response to large noncoronary collateral flow, not to low root pressure in valve surgery.
choiceNotes.d: Continuing root infusion with LV massage is for mild AR with **adequate** root pressure.
choiceNotes.e: The described sequence continues with retrograde and ostial delivery; the clamp is not released.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: During a long aortic valve procedure, cardioplegia is delivered by **direct cannulation of the coronary ostia**, with repeated cannulation maneuvers. Which late complication does the chapter warn about?

choices.text: Coronary sinus rupture
Calcium overload of the myocardium
Aortic valve regurgitation
Later coronary ostial stenosis
Left ventricular distention

explanation.text: Direct cannulation of the ostia (==especially multiple cannulation maneuvers==) ==may lead to later ostial stenosis==.

explanation.title: Cross-clamp > 90 min
explanation.text: Give **antegrade ostial** delivery at **every third** reinfusion, in addition to retrograde application every 20–30 min. The warm terminal reperfusion ("hot shot") can then be given antegrade via the **aortic root cannula** once the valve is repaired or replaced.
Coronary sinus rupture is a complication of **retrograde** cardioplegia, not of ostial cannulation.
One must remember that direct cannulation of the ostia (especially multiple cannulation maneuvers) may lead to later ostial stenosis.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 103

choiceNotes.a: Coronary sinus rupture is a complication of **retrograde** catheters.
choiceNotes.b: Calcium overload is a risk of the immature myocardium after ischemia-reperfusion, not of ostial cannulation.
choiceNotes.c: The warning about ostial cannulation concerns **ostial stenosis**.
choiceNotes.e: Distention is avoided by venting and LV massage; it is not the late complication of ostial cannulation.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: During a cardiac operation in a patient with **aortic regurgitation too mild to justify valve replacement**, an appropriate aortic root pressure **cannot be achieved** during cold cardioplegia. How are cold cardioplegia and the later reperfusion delivered?

choices.text: Cold cardioplegia via the root at higher flow; reperfusion through the root
Cold cardioplegia via the coronary ostia; reperfusion through the root
Cold cardioplegia via the root with LV massage; reperfusion retrograde
Cold cardioplegia retrograde; reperfusion abandoned in favour of clamp release
Cold cardioplegia retrograde; reperfusion exclusively retrograde via the coronary sinus

explanation.text: Cold cardioplegia is given ==retrogradely through the coronary sinus==, and the heart can be carried through warm hyperkalemic then normokalemic reperfusion ==exclusively retrograde==.

branches.label: root pressure not achievable
branches.text: **Retrograde** cold cardioplegia + **retrograde** reperfusion (warm hyperkalemic → normokalemic) until cardiac action fully resumes

explanation.text: cold cardioplegic solution is administered retrogradely through the coronary sinus.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: If root pressure cannot be achieved, the root route is replaced by **retrograde** delivery.
choiceNotes.b: Here the aorta is not opened; delivery is **retrograde** through the coronary sinus.
choiceNotes.c: Root infusion with LV massage applies when root pressure **is** adequate.
choiceNotes.d: Reperfusion is **not** abandoned; it is carried out exclusively retrograde.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A patient in **cardiogenic shock** is brought to the operating room shortly after **acute LAD occlusion**. Which element belongs to the myocardial management program described?

choices.text: Prolonged (20 min) controlled regional reperfusion of the LAD with hyperkalemic modified blood
Initial warm induction given antegrade only, for 5 minutes
An internal thoracic artery graft to the LAD instead of any vein graft
A single cold cardioplegic dose without further infusions
Immediate release of the clamp after the last distal anastomosis

explanation.text: The program includes ==prolonged (20 min) controlled regional reperfusion== of the LAD (or culprit vessel) with ==hyperkalemic modified blood==.

items: Initial controlled **warm** cardioplegia: **2.5 min antegrade + 2.5 min retrograde** (coronary sinus).
At least a **vein graft** to the LAD (or the culprit vessel).
**20 min** controlled **regional reperfusion** of the culprit artery with hyperkalemic modified blood.

explanation.text: Initial warm cardioplegia followed by usual cold cardioplegia produces quiescence; during grafting, intermittent cold infusions continue, **antegrade and retrograde alternately** or as dictated by ease of delivery or number of grafts.
Prolonged (20 min) controlled regional reperfusion with hyperkalemic modified blood of the LAD
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.b: Warm induction is **2.5 min antegrade and 2.5 min retrograde**; 5 min antegrade is the energy-depleted heart protocol.
choiceNotes.c: The program calls for **at least a vein graft** to the LAD.
choiceNotes.d: Cold cardioplegia is supplemented by **additional intermittent infusions** during grafting.
choiceNotes.e: The program includes **20 min** of controlled regional reperfusion of the culprit vessel.

stem: During CABG in a patient with long-standing severe coronary disease, the arrested heart **begins to show electromechanical activity** despite venting and multidose cardioplegia, from **large noncoronary collateral flow** washing out the cardioplegia. What is recommended?

choices.text: Increase CPB flow and give continuous warm cardioplegia
Release the clamp and complete the grafts on the beating heart
Cool to 20°C, reduce CPB flow to about 1 L/min/m^2^, and give more cold cardioplegia
Increase left ventricular vent suction and continue as usual
Give only retrograde cardioplegia at normothermia

explanation.text: At the first sign, the perfusate is made ==as cold as possible until the patient reaches 20°C==, CPB flow is reduced to ==about 1 L/min/m^2^==, and ==another dose of cold cardioplegia== is given.

steps.label: response
steps.text: Cool to **20°C** → perfusate 20°C, flow **about 1 L/min/m^2^** → repeat **cold cardioplegia**

explanation.text: Another dose of cold cardioplegia is then administered.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: CPB flow is **reduced** (about 1 L/min/m^2^), and **cold**, not warm, cardioplegia is given.
choiceNotes.b: The chapter keeps the heart arrested with cooling, low flow and more cold cardioplegia.
choiceNotes.d: Activity restarts **despite** venting; cooling and low flow are needed.
choiceNotes.e: The response is systemic cooling to **20°C** with another **cold** dose.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A critically ill patient with **active rheumatic pericarditis** needs **multiple-valve surgery** for aortic and mitral regurgitation. If cold cardioplegia is used, what else is necessary, and why?

choices.text: Continuous warm cardioplegia, because adhesions prevent cooling
Low-flow hypothermic perfusion and repeated infusions, because divided vascular adhesions add collateral flow
A single cardioplegic dose, because the inflamed myocardium tolerates ischemia well
Full-flow normothermic perfusion, because adhesions cause excessive bleeding
Retrograde delivery only, because aortic regurgitation prevents any root infusion

explanation.text: The extensive, ==vascular pericardial adhesions==, if divided, cause excessive bleeding and ==excessive collateral coronary flow==; with cold cardioplegia, ==low-flow hypothermic perfusion and repeated cardioplegic infusions== are necessary.
If cold cardioplegia is used, low-flow hypothermic perfusion and repeated cardioplegic infusions are necessary.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: The chapter specifies **cold** cardioplegia with low-flow **hypothermic** perfusion.
choiceNotes.c: **Repeated** cardioplegic infusions are necessary.
choiceNotes.d: Perfusion should be **low-flow** and **hypothermic**.
choiceNotes.e: The chapter does not restrict delivery to the retrograde route here; it requires low-flow hypothermic perfusion and repeated infusions.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass
source.loc: p. 104, Active Rheumatic Pericarditis Necessitating Multiple-Valve Surgery

stem: At **reoperative CABG**, a **patent internal thoracic artery (ITA) graft** is present. In most cases, how is it managed during the cardioplegic period, and what is the alternative?

choices.text: Left open routinely, with normothermic CPB and continuous warm cardioplegia
Ligated and divided permanently, with cardioplegia given only retrograde
Left open routinely, with antegrade root cardioplegia alone at 32°C
Identified, partially mobilized and occluded; or left open with CPB at 20°C–25°C
Fully mobilized and transposed before any cardioplegia is given

explanation.text: In most cases a patent ITA graft is ==identified by careful dissection, partially mobilized and occluded== during the cardioplegic period. Alternatively, it is ==left open with CPB at 20°C to 25°C==, frequent cardioplegia and **intermittent fibrillation**.
In most cases, a patent internal thoracic artery graft should be identified by careful dissection, partially mobilized, and occluded during the cardioplegic period.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: If left open, CPB is conducted at **20–25°C** with frequent cardioplegia and intermittent fibrillation.
choiceNotes.b: The ITA is **occluded** temporarily during the cardioplegic period, not divided; antegrade and retrograde infusions are complementary.
choiceNotes.c: If left open, CPB is at **20–25°C** with frequent cardioplegia and intermittent fibrillation.
choiceNotes.e: It is only **partially** mobilized and occluded.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: During **reoperative cardiac surgery**, more frequent cardioplegic infusions and/or a lower systemic perfusion temperature are advised. What is the reason given?

choices.text: Patent vein grafts always block antegrade delivery
The coronary sinus cannot be cannulated in reoperations
Reoperative hearts are always severely hypertrophied
Patent ITA grafts must be left open in every case
Because of adhesions, the myocardium rewarms more quickly than usual

explanation.text: ==Because of adhesions, the myocardium tends to rewarm more quickly than usual==, so more frequent cardioplegia, low systemic perfusion temperature, or both are appropriate.

items: Establish cardioplegic protection **early**, usually **before mobilization** of the cardiac mass.
Antegrade and retrograde infusions are **complementary**: place the retrograde catheter accurately (minimal sharp dissection over the **acute margin of the RV**, then posterior freeing dissection).
With **saphenous vein grafts left in place**, aortic root antegrade plus retrograde infusion seems the surest way to near-optimal delivery at induction.

explanation.text: Because of adhesions, the myocardium tends to rewarm more quickly than usual.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: With vein grafts in place, **antegrade root plus retrograde** infusion is the surest delivery; the stated reason for frequent dosing is faster rewarming.
choiceNotes.b: The retrograde catheter **can** be placed accurately via dissection over the acute margin of the RV.
choiceNotes.c: Hypertrophy is not the stated reason; **adhesions** cause faster rewarming.
choiceNotes.d: A patent ITA is usually **occluded**; leaving it open is only an alternative.
